outcomes.original: Filing step: Form the legal entity (LLC or corporation) with the California Secretary of State and obtain an EIN from the IRS. What to say: File Articles of Organization (LLC-1, $70) or Articles of Incorporation (ARTS-GS, $100) online at bizfile.sos.ca.gov, then apply for the federal EIN at irs.gov the same day. The EIN and entity name are required for the San Francisco business registration, bank account, lease signature, and all subsequent permit applications. File the Statement of Information with the Secretary of State within 90 days ($20 LLC / $25 corporation).

outcomes.original: Filing step: Register the business with the San Francisco Treasurer & Tax Collector to obtain a Business Account Number (BAN). What to say: Submit the business registration online at sftreasurer.org/business within 30 days of forming the entity. Provide the EIN, entity name, 767 Bush St address, and NAICS code 722511 (Full-Service Restaurants). Pay the tiered fee based on projected gross receipts ($55 minimum). The BAN is required by every other City department (Planning, DPH, DBI, SFPUC) before they will accept an application.

What to say: Describe the concept as a limited-service restaurant serving [cuisine type] to neighborhood residents and workers, operating [proposed hours]. outcomes.original: Filing step: Hire an architect licensed in California to prepare building permit plans for the tenant improvements, including DPH plan check sheets, mechanical hood drawings, plumbing for grease interceptor and hand sinks, electrical, and ADA compliance. What to say: Engage an architect experienced with San Francisco restaurant projects to design the kitchen, dining area, restrooms, and all code-required elements. The plans must be routed for simultaneous review by DBI, DPH, SFPUC (FOG), and Planning (zoning sign-off on the CUA). Include the occupancy calculation, exiting plan, accessibility path of travel, commercial hood with Type I suppression system, three-compartment sink, prep sink, handwash sinks at the kitchen and restroom, grease interceptor sized per SFPUC guidance, floor finishes, and equipment schedule. Submit the DPH plan check application ($828–$2,207) at the same time as or before the building permit to avoid delays.
outcomes.note: Records confirm architect-stamped plans, DPH fee range, and simultaneous submission, but do not list the specific plan elements or agencies named.

outcomes.original: Filing step: After the CUA is approved and the Motion is signed, file the building permit application with DBI, attaching the CUA Motion and all stamped plan sets from DPH, mechanical, plumbing, and electrical review. What to say: Submit the building permit online at dbiweb.sfgov.org, routing it to Planning (zoning sign-off on the approved CUA), DPH (health plan check), SFPUC (FOG interceptor), Fire (kitchen hood suppression), and any other required departments. Pay the permit fees (percentage of construction valuation, typically $800–$15,000). The permit will not be issued until Planning confirms the CUA is final (after the 30-day appeal period) and all plan corrections are completed. Licensed subcontractors will pull separate electrical, plumbing, and mechanical permits as needed.

outcomes.original: Filing step: During construction, schedule the DPH pre-final inspection at ~80% completion and the final health inspection once all equipment is installed, to obtain the Health Permit to Operate. What to say: Contact your DPH plan reviewer at least two weeks before each inspection to book the appointment. At the pre-final, the inspector will identify any missing sinks, finishes, or equipment; correct those items before the final inspection. At the final, demonstrate that one employee holds a Food Manager Certification, the kitchen is clean and ready, all plumbing has hot water, and the menu matches the approved plans. The permit to operate ($470 application fee in FY 2026–27, $0 annual license fee for 2026–28) is issued after the inspector approves; you cannot serve the public before it is issued.

outcomes.original: Estimated time: 120 to 300 days. Estimated government cost: $2,803 to $18,850. Notes: This range is the time to obtain the three approvals (CUA, health permit, building permit) when they are granted, not the time to a denial or withdrawal. The Conditional Use Authorization is the critical path: approximately 120–300 days from filing to approval including pre-application meeting, environmental review, neighborhood notification if required, Planning Commission hearing, and the 30-day appeal period. The building permit (14–120 days) and health permit (14–45 days) follow sequentially because DBI will not issue the building permit until the CUA is final, and DPH will not issue the health permit until construction and final inspection are complete. Government fees include CUA application (estimated $3,000–$3,500 based on typical 2023 rates, adjusted annually), building permit ($800–$15,000 depending on construction value), DPH plan check ($828–$2,500), health permit to operate ($470), business registration ($55–$700), entity formation ($70–$150), and small fees for EDD, fictitious business name, sign permit, and FOG program. This estimate excludes construction costs, architect fees, insurance, and any deposits. The 779 Bush St CUA (14 m away, filed November 2022 for a laundromat-to-bar conversion) has been pending with no decision as of the data cut-off, suggesting that laundromat-removal CUAs may face longer review or neighbor opposition; confirm the likely timeline at the pre-application meeting.
